analogy.p: Imagine students walking along a corridor and a collision happens whenever two students bump into each other. In a nearly empty corridor (low concentration) bumps are rare; in the same corridor at the end of lessons (high concentration) there are far more bumps every second, even though everyone walks at the same speed. This maps onto particles: more particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions, so a greater rate of successful collisions. It breaks down because real particles only react if they collide with at least the activation energy and in the right orientation, whereas every student bump counts as a bump.

bullets: The two methods are **gas collection** (for example magnesium or calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid) and **turbidity/colour change** (sodium thiosulfate with hydrochloric acid, the disappearing cross).
The **independent variable** is the concentration of one reactant; the **dependent variable** is the rate, found from volume of gas against time or from the time for the cross to disappear.

The conclusion is always: **as concentration increases, the rate of reaction increases**, because there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent, so more successful collisions per second.

Apparatus and techniques covered by this practical include accurate measurement of volumes (pipette, burette, measuring cylinder, gas syringe), use of a stopwatch, heating-free safe handling of acids and gases, and recording results in a table.

Related spec content you must also be able to use: calculating **mean rate = quantity of reactant used or product formed ÷ time taken**, units g/s, cm3/s or mol/s, and (Higher tier) drawing **tangents** to find the rate at a particular time.
Typical mark allocations: 1 mark for a hazard or a control variable, 2 marks for a conclusion with explanation, up to 6 marks for describing the whole investigation in the correct order.
Plan the answer around a repeating structure: **what you change, what you measure, what you keep the same, how you measure it, what you expect and why**.
core.h: What the specification and the required practical ask you to do
core.p: AQA Chemistry **Required Practical 5** says: investigate how changes in **concentration** affect the **rates of reactions** by a method involving **measuring the volume of a gas produced** and a method involving a **change in colour or turbidity**. You therefore need to know two complete methods, the variables, the hazards, how to turn raw results into a rate, how to draw and read the graphs, and how to explain the conclusion using **collision theory**. Examiners also ask about this practical in the written papers (Paper 2), mostly through method, variables, graph and evaluation questions, and it is worth around 15% of the total GCSE marks across all required practicals.

bullets: Sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid: **Na2S2O3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + SO2(g) + S(s) + H2O(l)**. The yellow-white solid sulfur is a **precipitate**; the reaction mixture goes from clear to cloudy.
Magnesium + hydrochloric acid: **Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)**. Hydrogen is almost insoluble in water, so the gas volume collected is reliable.

Calcium carbonate (marble chips) + hydrochloric acid: **CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)**. Carbon dioxide is slightly soluble in water, so a gas syringe is better than collection over water.
The thiosulfate reaction is easy to repeat many times quickly because it finishes within a minute or two and the product stays in the flask.
The Mg/HCl reaction gives a full rate-against-time curve, from which you can find both mean rates and (Higher tier) rates at different instants by drawing tangents.
A **precipitate** is an insoluble solid that forms in a solution during a reaction; **turbidity** is cloudiness caused by tiny suspended solid particles.
In all cases the reaction rate is what is being compared; the chemistry of the reaction itself is not changed by the investigation, only the concentration is.
core.h: The two reactions you will use and why each suits the job
core.p: Both reactions are chosen because something changes that you can **observe and time**. In the thiosulfate reaction a solid **sulfur precipitate** makes the solution cloudy (turbid), so the time taken for a marked cross to be hidden measures the rate. In the magnesium (or marble chips) reaction a **gas** is made, so the gas volume at timed intervals measures the rate. Choosing a reaction with an easy-to-detect change is the first thing a mark scheme wants you to justify.

bullets: Draw a **black cross** on a piece of white paper and place a **conical flask** on top of it. Always use the same cross and the same flask.
Use a **measuring cylinder (or burette/pipette for more accuracy)** to put a measured volume of sodium thiosulfate solution into the flask, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm3 in separate trials.
Add **water** so that the total volume of thiosulfate + water is the same every time (e.g. 50 cm3). This makes thiosulfate concentration the only thing that changes.
Measure a fixed volume of dilute **hydrochloric acid** (e.g. 10 cm3) in a separate measuring cylinder; the concentration of the acid must be the same every time.
Add the acid to the flask and **start the stopwatch at the instant the acid is added**; swirl the flask once to mix.
Look down through the solution from above. **Stop the stopwatch when the cross is no longer visible**. Record the time in seconds.

Pour the contents away safely (in a fume cupboard or a well-ventilated area, then wash the flask well), and repeat for each concentration. Do each concentration at least **three times** and calculate a mean.
Calculate the rate as **1 ÷ time** (units s⁻¹) because the same amount of sulfur is formed in every case when the cross disappears.
Higher tier link: since the same amount of precipitate is needed to hide the cross every time, **rate is proportional to 1/time**, not to time itself.
core.h: Method 1: sodium thiosulfate and acid (the disappearing cross), step by step
core.p: This is a **colour/turbidity** method. The idea is that the sulfur precipitate gradually hides a cross drawn on paper under the flask, and you time how long it takes for the cross to just disappear when viewed from above. A higher concentration of thiosulfate produces sulfur faster, so the cross disappears sooner and the time is shorter. To make a fair comparison you must change only the concentration of thiosulfate and keep the total volume the same by adding **water**.

bullets: Measure a fixed volume of dilute hydrochloric acid (e.g. 50 cm3) using a **measuring cylinder** and pour it into a conical flask. Use a different concentration in each experiment (e.g. 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm3).
Clean a piece of **magnesium ribbon** with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer, and cut the same length (e.g. 2 cm, ≈0.05 g) for each trial.
Set up the delivery tube and **gas syringe** (check it moves freely and starts at 0 cm3). Everything must be airtight.
Drop in the magnesium, **immediately put the bung in** and **start the stopwatch**. Gas escaping before the bung is fitted would give a false low volume.
Record the **gas volume every 10 seconds** (or every 15 s for slower reactions) until the volume stops changing.
Repeat for each concentration; for each, plot or calculate **volume against time**.

Check that the magnesium is the **limiting reactant**: 0.05 g ÷ 24 g/mol = 0.0021 mol Mg, needing 0.0042 mol HCl; 50 cm3 of 0.2 mol/dm3 gives 0.010 mol HCl, so acid is in excess even at the lowest concentration and the final volume of H2 (≈50 cm3 at room temperature and pressure) is the same each time.

An **inverted measuring cylinder over water** is an alternative to the syringe: fill it with water, invert it in a trough, and put the delivery tube underneath; read the volume from the water level. It is less precise than a syringe, and CO2 would partially dissolve.
A gas syringe can stick, so tap it gently or lubricate the plunger; the maximum volume (often 100 cm3) must not be exceeded.
core.h: Method 2: measuring the volume of gas produced
core.p: This is the **gas collection** method. A fixed mass of magnesium ribbon (or marble chips) reacts with hydrochloric acid of known concentration and the gas is collected in a **gas syringe** (or an inverted measuring cylinder full of water in a trough). The volume is read at regular time intervals, typically every 10 seconds, until the reaction stops. Repeating with acid of different concentration gives a set of curves you can compare.

bullets: Set up a conical flask on a **balance** with the acid; add marble chips and place a loose plug of **cotton wool** in the neck to stop acid spray escaping but let the gas out.
Start the stopwatch, record the mass every 10–30 seconds until it is constant.
Plot **mass lost (g) against time (s)**; the curve has the same shape as the gas-volume graph.
Rate = mass of CO2 lost ÷ time, with units **g/s**.
Advantages: no gas syringe or leaks to worry about. Disadvantages: the balance must be sensitive (0.01 g or better), and the mass changes are small for low gas density.
Because the reaction is exothermic and water vapour can escape, there can be small systematic errors.
core.h: Method 3 (alternative): mass loss as gas escapes
core.p: When a gas is made in an open flask, the flask and contents lose mass because the gas escapes. If the flask is on a balance, the **mass reading falls** and the rate can be found from mass lost against time. This is useful for carbon dioxide (marble chips and acid) because CO2 is dense and easily measured this way, but it is not suitable for hydrogen because the mass lost is tiny.

bullets: **Independent variable:** concentration of acid (gas method) or of sodium thiosulfate (cross method), in mol/dm3 or as volume of stock solution with water making a constant total volume.
**Dependent variable:** gas volume at set times, or time for the cross to disappear (and so the rate).

**Control variables:** temperature of solutions (use a water bath or the same room), volume of solution, mass/length and surface area of magnesium or size of marble chips, concentration of the other reactant, the same flask, cross and observer, same way of mixing.
Temperature matters because rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise, so even a 3 °C difference between experiments can distort the results.
Surface area is controlled by using ribbon of identical length and thickness, or chips of the same size.
Using a **fixed total volume** is crucial: if you only add less thiosulfate without water, you change the volume as well as concentration.

State how to measure each variable and **with which apparatus**: e.g. gas volume with a gas syringe (resolution 1 cm3), time with a stopwatch (resolution 0.1 s), volume of liquids with a measuring cylinder or pipette.
core.h: Variables: what you change, measure and control
core.p: A valid investigation changes **one thing at a time**. The **independent variable** is the one you deliberately change (concentration); the **dependent variable** is what you measure as a result (time or volume of gas); everything else must be kept the same so that any difference is caused only by the concentration. Mark schemes want specific control variables with the way to control them, not just 'keep it fair'.

bullets: **Mean rate** = total change ÷ total time. Example: 48 cm3 in 60 s → 0.80 cm3/s.
**Rate at a given time:** (Higher tier) draw a **tangent** to the curve at that time and find its gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.
**Initial rate** is the rate at t = 0 and is the steepest part of the curve; compare initial rates between experiments to test the effect of concentration.
For the cross method use **rate = 1 ÷ time**, since the same amount of sulfur is needed each time.
The rate **decreases** during a reaction because reactants are used up, so the concentration falls and collisions become less frequent.
A reaction is finished when the graph becomes **horizontal (gradient zero)**: no more product is made because one reactant (the limiting reactant) has all been used.
Units must always be stated; a bare number scores no mark in a calculation question.
core.p: The **rate of a reaction** tells you how fast reactants are used up or products formed. The spec gives **mean rate of reaction = quantity of reactant used ÷ time taken** or **quantity of product formed ÷ time taken**. The quantity can be a mass in grams, a volume of gas in cm3 or an amount in moles, so the units are g/s, cm3/s or mol/s (and for the cross method, s⁻¹).

bullets: Volume–time curves start steep (fast rate) then **curve over and level off** as reactants are used up.
A **steeper initial gradient** means a faster initial rate – the higher concentration curve is always steeper and reaches the plateau sooner.
If the acid is in excess and the magnesium is limiting, **all curves level off at the same volume** because the same amount of product forms.
To use a tangent at a point: place a ruler so it touches the curve at only that point, matching the slope on both sides, and draw a long straight line; use a large triangle to calculate the gradient.
For the 1/t against concentration plot, a **straight line through the origin** shows rate is **directly proportional** to concentration.
Mark **anomalous results** (points far off the pattern) and exclude them from the mean or line of best fit, saying why.
Read-off questions: take values from the graph to 1 small square, and show the lines you draw on the graph.
core.p: Graphs make the pattern in the results clear. For the gas method plot **volume of gas (y) against time (x)**; for the cross method plot **rate (1/time) against concentration**. In every case use a sensible scale that fills at least half the grid, label the axes with quantity and unit, plot points accurately and draw a smooth **line of best fit** (a smooth curve for volume–time, a straight line through the origin if rate is directly proportional to concentration).

bullets: Say '**more frequent collisions**' or 'more collisions per second', not just 'more collisions', otherwise the mark is lost.
Concentration does **not** change how fast the particles move or the energy of each collision; those depend on temperature.
A **successful collision** is one in which particles collide with at least the **activation energy** and with the right orientation.
In the thiosulfate reaction doubling the concentration of thiosulfate roughly halves the time, so the rate doubles (rate ∝ concentration for this reaction).
In the gas method, double the concentration of acid gives a steeper initial gradient, but not necessarily double the rate for all reactions – describe what the data actually show.
For gases, increasing **pressure** has the same effect as concentration: more particles per unit volume.
Link: using the idea of **collision theory** in all rate questions is expected from Grade 4 upwards.
core.h: Conclusion and explanation using collision theory
core.p: The data show that **increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction**. The explanation (always asked, usually for 2–3 marks) is: in a more concentrated solution there are **more particles of the reactant in the same volume**, so the particles are **closer together**, so they **collide more frequently**. A higher frequency of collisions means a higher frequency of **successful collisions** per second, so more product is made in a given time.

bullets: Concentration after dilution = stock concentration × (volume of stock ÷ total volume).
Example: 30 cm3 of 0.10 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate in a total of 60 cm3 → 0.10 × 30 ÷ 60 = **0.050 mol/dm3**.
Concentration in g/dm3 = mass (g) ÷ volume (dm3); mol/dm3 = (g/dm3) ÷ relative formula mass.
Making the dilution series: put the volume of stock in the flask, add water to make the total constant (e.g. 50 cm3) and mix before adding the acid.
Use a **burette or pipette** for greater accuracy than a measuring cylinder when measuring small volumes.
When the acid is also added, the final total includes the acid volume, so state the final concentration in the mixture or just state the volume of stock used.
core.p: You need to be able to work out the concentration of a diluted solution and to prepare solutions of different concentrations from a stock. **Concentration (mol/dm3) = amount (mol) ÷ volume (dm3)**, and to convert cm3 to dm3 divide by 1000. When you dilute, the amount of solute stays the same but the volume increases, so concentration falls in proportion.

bullets: **Dilute hydrochloric acid** is an irritant to eyes and skin at the concentrations used – wear **eye protection (goggles)** and wash splashes off with water immediately.

**Sulfur dioxide gas** is produced in the thiosulfate reaction; it is toxic and can trigger **asthma attacks** – use small volumes, work in a well-ventilated area or **fume cupboard**, and have people with asthma avoid it.
**Hydrogen** is flammable (forms an explosive mixture with air) – no naked flames nearby.
**Magnesium ribbon** is flammable if heated; keep it away from flames. Sandpaper creates dust – wear goggles.
**Glassware** (conical flask, gas syringe) can break – use trays, keep the apparatus clamped and remove broken glass safely.
Do not stopper a flask tightly with no outlet: a rising gas pressure could pop the bung off. Connect the delivery tube and syringe before adding the reagents.
Dispose of the mixture by pouring it down the sink with plenty of water (if allowed) or into the waste container as the teacher instructs.
A good answer: 'Sulfur dioxide is toxic and may trigger asthma, so carry out the reaction in a fume cupboard.'
core.p: Risk assessments are part of every required practical. Name the **hazard**, say what harm it can cause, and give a **specific control measure**. Marks are lost for vague answers such as 'be careful'. In this practical the main risks come from the acid, from the toxic sulfur dioxide gas and from the flammable hydrogen, and a good risk assessment also thinks about glassware and spills.

bullets: **Resolution** is the smallest change an instrument can detect (e.g. 1 cm3 on a syringe, 0.01 s on a stopwatch); greater resolution gives more precise data.

The biggest source of error in the cross method is judging **when the cross disappears** – different observers will see it at different moments; use the same person, or a light sensor and data logger.
Reaction time delays (≈0.2–0.5 s) in starting/stopping the watch are more significant for short times, so use larger volumes/lower concentrations for longer times.
Gas can be lost before the bung is fitted, giving volumes that are too low – put the bung in immediately.
Repeat each concentration and discard **anomalies**; calculate the **mean** to reduce the effect of random errors.
Use the **same flask, same cross and same lighting** to remove variation in how the cross looks.
Temperature rises slightly during the reaction (exothermic); using a water bath or a large volume of solution reduces this.
core.p: Evaluating the experiment is always examined. **Accuracy** is how close a measurement is to the true value; **precision** is how close repeated measurements are to each other; **repeatable** means the same person gets the same results with the same method; **reproducible** means a different person or method gets the same. Errors can be **random** (unpredictable, reduced by repeating and taking a mean) or **systematic** (a consistent offset, e.g. a faulty balance).

bullets: Use a **data logger, pH probe or colorimeter/light sensor** to detect the endpoint objectively and record continuously.
Use a **water bath** to hold the temperature constant, and pre-warm or pre-cool solutions to the same temperature before mixing.
Use a **burette or pipette** instead of measuring cylinders for smaller uncertainties in volume.
Take **more concentrations** (at least five) over a wider range to see the pattern more clearly, and repeat more times.
Extend the method to **temperature**: keep concentration constant and vary the temperature of the solutions, e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50 °C, using the same cross method.
Extend to **surface area**: use marble chips of different sizes (or powder) with the same mass of CaCO3 and the same acid, and compare the mass-loss or gas-volume rate.
Extend to **catalysts**: add a small amount of manganese(IV) oxide to hydrogen peroxide and collect the oxygen made, comparing with the uncatalysed reaction.
core.p: Questions often ask how the experiment could be improved or how to extend it to test a different factor. The best answers say **what** to change and **why** it improves reliability, accuracy or validity.

bullets: Rate and **yield** are different: concentration can increase the rate without changing the final amount of product (in an irreversible reaction).
In **industry**, higher concentrations and pressures increase rate but add costs and safety risk, so conditions are a compromise.
**Tangent method (Higher tier):** gradient = Δy ÷ Δx, e.g. a tangent from (0, 6 cm3) to (60 s, 42 cm3) gives (42 − 6) ÷ 60 = 0.60 cm3/s.
**Mole conversion:** 24 dm3 of any gas at room temperature and pressure = 1 mole, so 48 cm3 H2 = 0.0020 mol; this lets you express a rate in mol/s.
The **order of the reaction** is not tested at GCSE, but plotting rate against concentration and seeing a straight line through the origin is accepted as direct proportionality.
The same practical skills are reused for the **required practical on electrolysis**, **titrations** and **energy changes** (variables, repeats, means, uncertainty).
Exothermic reactions raise temperature, which itself speeds the reaction – a reason to use a water bath.
core.h: Linking to other topics and Higher tier extensions
core.p: The rate practical underpins several other topics. You apply **collision theory** and **activation energy** (4.6.1.2), **catalysts** (4.6.1.4), **reversible reactions and equilibrium** (4.6.2) and the **Haber process** (4.10), where compromise conditions balance rate and yield. Skills from maths – substituting into rate equations, drawing tangents, proportionality and unit conversion – are also assessed.

bullets: **Describe:** give a numbered method: apparatus, quantities, what to change, what to measure, how to repeat. Include units and volumes.
**Explain:** use 'because', link a cause to a consequence – 'more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions'.
**Plot:** choose axes with the independent variable on x; use over half the grid; label with units; points as small crosses; a smooth line of best fit.
**Calculate:** write the formula, substitute, answer with units; check against the data trend.
**Evaluate:** mention accuracy, precision, anomalies, number of repeats, control of variables and suggest a specific improvement with a reason.
**Safety:** name the hazard, the harm and the control measure.
Always say what stays the same – a six-mark answer should name at least three control variables.
Re-read the question: 'time for the cross to disappear' – a shorter time means a faster rate.
core.p: The required practical often appears as a **6-mark 'describe how' question**, a data table to plot, and an evaluation of the results. The command words **describe, explain, suggest, evaluate** each need a different approach, and examiners reward answers with the correct sequence and specific values.

exam: **Command words:** 'describe' = give the method in order with quantities; 'explain' = give reasons using collision theory; 'suggest' = apply your knowledge to the context; 'evaluate' = weigh strengths and weaknesses and reach a judgement.
**1 mark:** one control variable, one hazard with its control, or one correct unit (cm3/s).
**2 marks:** conclusion with reason – 'As concentration increases the rate increases because there are more particles in the same volume so more frequent collisions.'
**3–4 marks:** describe how to measure the rate of a reaction that makes a gas – apparatus, timing, repeats, calculation.

**6 marks:** a clear, logical method with measured volumes, same temperature, how to dilute, what to measure, repeats, calculations and a safety point; if the question has a level-of-response mark scheme, aim for a coherent chain of steps.
**Graph tips:** independent variable on the x-axis, scale over half the page, label units, plot with crosses, draw a smooth curve (not dot-to-dot), and show tangent construction lines.
**Calculation tips:** show the equation, substitute with units, give the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures (usually 2–3), and include units.
**Data tips:** use the table to spot patterns (e.g. time halves when concentration doubles); quote data in your answer (e.g. 'time falls from 100 s to 50 s').
**Evaluation phrases:** 'repeat and calculate a mean', 'use a more precise measuring instrument', 'use a light sensor to remove human judgement', 'use a water bath to keep the temperature constant'.
**Common traps:** forgetting to keep total volume constant; confusing precision and accuracy; saying 'faster reaction means longer time'.

mistakes.r: The solid precipitate is sulfur; sulfur dioxide is a toxic gas that dissolves/escapes.
mistakes.w: The solid formed in the thiosulfate reaction is sulfur dioxide.

mistakes.r: Keep the total volume constant by adding water, so that only the concentration changes.
mistakes.w: Add less thiosulfate to lower the concentration (without adding water).

mistakes.r: Particle speed depends on temperature; higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions.
mistakes.w: Higher concentration makes the particles move faster.

mistakes.r: Rate = quantity ÷ time, or 1 ÷ time for the cross method; a shorter time means a faster rate.
More frequent collisions (or successful collisions per second) – frequency is the key word.
mistakes.w: More collisions, so the rate is faster.

mistakes.r: Name the variables: temperature, volume of acid, mass/length of magnesium, surface area, same cross and observer.
It levels off because one reactant (the limiting reactant) has been used up, so no more product forms.
mistakes.w: The graph levels off because the reaction runs out of time.

mistakes.r: A tangent touches the curve at one point only; its gradient is calculated with a large triangle.
mistakes.w: Draw a tangent by joining two data points with a ruler.

mistakes.r: Name the hazard and control: sulfur dioxide is toxic → fume cupboard; acid irritant → goggles.
mistakes.w: Wear safety clothing to be safe (no hazard named).

summary: AQA Required Practical 5 asks you to investigate how concentration changes the rate of a reaction using one gas-volume method and one colour/turbidity method (disappearing cross), then to calculate rates, plot and interpret graphs, control variables safely and explain the result with collision theory. It matters because it combines practical skills, calculation and theory in one commonly examined context.

terms.d: How fast reactants are used up or products are formed; measured as the change in quantity per unit time.
Quantity of reactant used or product formed divided by the time taken (e.g. cm3/s, g/s, mol/s).
The rate at the very start of the reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent at t = 0 or from 1 ÷ time for the cross to disappear.
The amount of solute in a given volume of solution, in mol/dm3 or g/dm3.
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions react; here the sulfur formed from thiosulfate and acid.
The cloudiness of a liquid caused by fine suspended solid particles; it stops light passing straight through.
The variable the investigator deliberately changes (here concentration).
The variable measured as the outcome (volume of gas or time taken).
A variable that is kept the same so it does not affect the results (temperature, volume, surface area).
A straight line drawn to touch a curve at one point; its gradient is the rate of reaction at that time (Higher tier).
Chemical reactions can only happen when reacting particles collide with sufficient energy; rate depends on the frequency and energy of collisions.
The minimum energy that particles must have to react when they collide.
The reactant that is completely used up first, so it determines the maximum amount of product formed.
The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect.
The same investigator gets the same results using the same method and equipment.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results and is usually excluded from the mean.

worked.ans: (a) 0.80 cm3/s (b) 0.15 cm3/s (c) The rate is lower because the concentration of the reactants has fallen, so there are fewer particles per unit volume and fewer successful collisions per second.
worked.q: [4 marks] 48 cm3 of hydrogen is collected in the first 60 s of a reaction and a total of 57 cm3 after 120 s. (a) Calculate the mean rate in the first 60 s. (b) Calculate the mean rate between 60 s and 120 s. (c) Explain the difference.
steps: (b) Volume in second minute = 57 − 48 = 9 cm3; rate = 9 ÷ 60.
(c) The reaction slows as the acid and magnesium are used up, so concentration falls and collisions are less frequent.

worked.ans: (a) 0.050 mol/dm3 (b) 0.030 s⁻¹ (c) The rate is directly proportional to the concentration: doubling the concentration halves the time and doubles the rate, because there are twice as many particles in the same volume, so collisions are twice as frequent.
worked.q: [5 marks] In a thiosulfate/acid experiment, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm3 of 0.10 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate were each made up to 50 cm3 with water, then 10 cm3 of acid was added. The times for the cross to vanish were 100 s, 50 s, 33 s, 25 s and 20 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of thiosulfate in the mixture when 30 cm3 was used. (b) Calculate the rate (1/t) for 30 cm3. (c) State the conclusion.
steps: (c) 1/t values are 0.010, 0.020, 0.030, 0.040, 0.050 s⁻¹: each is directly proportional to the volume (and so the concentration) of thiosulfate.

worked.ans: Model answer: Use the same volume (50 cm3) of acid at different concentrations in a flask at the same temperature. Add an identical piece of magnesium ribbon, quickly fit the bung with a gas syringe attached and start a stopwatch. Record the gas volume every 10 seconds until the reaction finishes. Repeat for each concentration and repeat each experiment to find a mean. Plot volume against time for each concentration and compare initial gradients; the steeper the line, the faster the rate. Wear goggles and keep flames away because hydrogen is flammable.
worked.q: [6 marks] Describe how you would investigate the effect of the concentration of hydrochloric acid on the rate of reaction with magnesium by measuring the volume of gas produced.
steps: Measure 50 cm3 of acid of one concentration with a measuring cylinder and pour into a conical flask; keep the temperature constant.
Add a 2 cm length of cleaned magnesium ribbon, immediately fit the bung connected to a gas syringe and start the stopwatch.
Record the volume of gas every 10 s until it stops increasing.
Repeat with acid of different concentrations (e.g. 0.2–1.0 mol/dm3), keeping volume, temperature and mass/length of magnesium the same.
Repeat each concentration at least three times and calculate a mean; plot volume against time and compare gradients / calculate rates.
Safety: wear goggles; hydrogen is flammable so no flames.
